passage:
For forty-one years, Ida Brannock walked out to the white box on the schoolhouse lawn in Wendle Cross at nine each morning, read the two instruments inside, a rain gauge and a thermometer, and wrote both figures in a handwritten ledger begun in 1938. In all that time the record shows one gap: eleven blank lines one February, when a fall on the ice kept her in hospital. Her rule was that no other person's figures went into the ledger, so the lines stayed empty.

This spring, at seventy-eight, she stepped down as keeper. The idea of a sensor came from the district weather office at Lowmarch, which had set one beside her box on trial the year before; its letter to the parish council said the machine would need nobody on the lawn each morning. Ida herself, she told the council, had one wish: that the record go on. The choice of whose hand kept it, she said, was theirs.

At the meeting, Neve Callan, who teaches the older class at the village school, offered her pupils instead: thirty of them, taking the nine o'clock reading in turns. The office had already said it would keep taking hand figures as long as they reached Lowmarch each month and passed its checks. The council voted for the pupils, its chair explaining that a record kept by thirty hands would outlast any single keeper.

The sensor went back to Lowmarch in April, and the pupils took charge of the ledger. Before the first morning, Neve opened it to the eleven blank lines and taught the class Ida's rule: write down only what you have read yourself.

On a wet morning in May, a nine-year-old named Pell Arden read the thermometer, wrote the figure, then crossed the lawn a second time to check it before the ink was dry. Her figures sit directly under Ida's, in the same ruled columns. In the pupils' first three months, the ledger has no blank line.

passage:
For many summers Tamsin Rowe has led a July walk through the Hatherby cutting, where a railway once ran between an old platform and a brick footbridge. Volunteers with red torches walk it in about 42 minutes, marking each green light on a map. Every light is a wingless female glow-worm. What she needs is a tall grass stem to climb after full dark, where she glows to draw flying males; her larvae live in the turf and feed on snails. Rowe's first walk found 35, and the usual total is now about ninety.

That spring the Hatherby Line Trust made several changes to the cutting. In March it put up 23 solar lamps at the platform end. In April it widened the path and laid gravel along it. In May its contractor did the mowing of the banks, usually left until September. And because the trust now locks the platform gate at ten, the walk was moved an hour earlier, to half past nine.

Last July the count fell to 16. The trust's first step was to have the gravel raked back from the foot of each bank and the bare strip returfed.

It had been a dry spring, and the dry weather held into June, so Rowe laid 28 snail boards along the banks. They came up crowded. She then repeated the walk at the old hour of half past ten and found much the same low total. On the maps, a steep strip below the footbridge, beyond reach of the mowing, looked just like the mown banks beside it. Every missing light lay at the platform end, within reach of the lamps; past the last lamp the banks shone as thickly as ever, right down to the new gravel.

The trust has switched the lamps off for June and July. But the field behind the platform has since been sold, and plans for sixty houses show street lights along its edge, a few yards from the bank where the females climb. The planning hearing is in March.

passage:
The radio warned of frost at supper: minus four by dawn, with the apricots in full blossom. Tomas looked over the blossoms on the corner tree first, the old tree his father had planted by the gate, and then read the thermometer nailed to the gate. After that he walked down to the young trees in the far row and came back by the barn to count the cans of oil: eleven, enough for the burners under half the orchard.

His plan was a ring of burners round the corner tree, which gave the best fruit on the place, and the rest in the far row, where he thought the cold settled first. He drew the loaded cart down from the barn himself, and I helped him set each burner with care.

Only then did he look across the lane at Mrs. Odell's orchard. She had judged that the cold would hold off until her trees were past blossom, and had let her oil order wait; now she stood at her gate with forty trees and nothing to light them with. Tomas pulled the burners out of the ring round the corner tree, put half the cans back on the cart, and called across that they would share what there was. I went with him to help.

We spent the night carrying oil across the lane wherever it was needed, guarding two orchards with one orchard's oil. The corner tree, out of reach of every burner now, stood pale and alone in the dark. Near four the frost was white on the lane and the thermometer touched minus five.

By morning Mrs. Odell's trees had come through, and the far row was saved. The corner tree had lost every blossom below the height of a man. The radio put the next frost in April, after the fruit had set, so the burners would wait in the barn until next spring before being lit again. Still in his boots, Tomas was back across the lane to ask how her trees had fared. If anyone asks me what kind of man my uncle is, I tell them about that morning.
